title: Weary with toil: the sleepless night
short: The poet, exhausted by travel, goes to bed only to find his mind sets off on another journey towards the absent friend.
body: Sonnets 27 and 28 form a pair on sleeplessness during absence, followed by the famous 29. They imply that the poet is travelling away from the friend (see Sonnets 48-51). The insomniac lover was a convention of Petrarchan verse: Petrarch's Rime and Sidney's Astrophil and Stella (e.g. sonnets 38-39, the address to sleep) supply models. Shakespeare's version is notably physical, opening with tired limbs before moving to the mind's 'journey'.

title: The dear respose [repose]
short: The bed is the precious resting place for limbs tired by travel; the archive's 'respose' is a misprint for 'repose'.
body: The line stands in apposition to 'my bed': the bed is the 'dear repose', i.e. the welcome rest, for tired limbs. The archive text reads 'respose', an error for the standard reading 'repose' (Quarto 'repose'). 'Dear' means precious and longed-for; it may also suggest costly, since the rest is never in fact granted. The line's slow, heavy rhythm enacts the tired body sinking into bed, before the mind's restlessness takes over in line 3. Readers using the archive should keep the correct spelling in mind when quoting.

title: travel / travail
short: The Quarto's 'trauaill' means both travel and travail (toil); the two were not yet distinct words.
body: In 1609 'travel' and 'travail' were spelling variants of one word, and the Quarto prints 'trauaill'. The sense here is both: limbs tired by a journey and by labour (the 'toil' of line 1). The doubleness matters because the sonnet sets the body's journey against the mind's 'journey in my head' and the body's work against the mind's work. Modern editions must choose a spelling, which loses one sense; Booth discusses the pun at length.

title: a journey in my head
short: As soon as the body rests, the mind begins its own travel towards the friend, so work begins again.
body: Line 4 plays on 'work': the mind is set to work just as the body's work has 'expired' (ended, with a hint of dying, as in the expiry of a lease). The neat symmetry of body and mind is the structure of the whole poem and is summed up in the couplet ('by day my limbs, by night my mind'). Vendler notes how the 'journey' becomes a 'pilgrimage' in line 6, raising the friend to a sacred object.

title: Intend
short: 'Intend' means set out on, direct their course towards, as well as purpose.
body: From Latin intendere, to stretch towards or direct one's course. The thoughts 'intend' a pilgrimage both in the sense that they plan it and that they actually set off towards the friend 'from far where I abide' (from the distant place where I am staying). The older sense of directed motion is recorded in the OED. The physical motion of the thoughts across distance is the point: the body lies still while the mind travels, the paradox on which the whole sonnet turns.

title: zealous pilgrimage
short: The lover's thoughts become devout pilgrims travelling to the beloved as to a shrine.
body: 'Zealous' means ardent, fervent, with religious overtones (zeal for God). Representing love as pilgrimage and the beloved as a saint is a Petrarchan commonplace; Shakespeare stages it in the 'palmers' sonnet' shared by Romeo and Juliet (1.5). After the Reformation, pilgrimage carried some Catholic colouring, which lends the image a hint of forbidden or excessive devotion. The pilgrimage keeps the eyes 'open wide' (l. 7), so devotion is also insomnia.

anchor: darkness which the blind do see
title: Looking on darkness which the blind do see
short: With eyes open in the dark, the poet sees only what the blind see: nothing but darkness.
body: The paradox of seeing darkness prepares for the 'imaginary sight' of the next line, which sees what the eyes cannot. The blind are said to 'see' darkness, so the lover is for the moment as good as blind. The line's heavy monosyllables and the long 'o' sounds of 'Looking on darkness' slow the verse to the pace of a sleepless night. The paradox of sight in darkness recurs in Sonnet 43 ('When most I wink, then do mine eyes best see').

title: imaginary sight
short: The soul's power of imagination, which can 'see' images of absent things; not 'unreal' sight.
body: 'Imaginary' here means belonging to the imagination (the faculty that forms images), not simply false. In Renaissance faculty psychology the imagination or 'fancy' presented images to the soul independently of the senses, particularly in sleep and dreams. Shakespeare uses the same idea in Henry V's Prologue, asking the audience to work their 'imaginary forces'. The soul's sight replaces the 'sightless view' (l. 10) of the eyes.

title: thy shadow
short: The friend's image or ghostly likeness; the Quarto reads 'their shadow', which editors emend to 'thy'.
body: 'Shadow' in Elizabethan English meant an image, reflection, portrait or phantom, as opposed to the 'substance' (compare Sonnet 53, 'What is your substance, whereof are you made, / That millions of strange shadows on you tend?'). The 1609 Quarto prints 'their shadow', one of several places where 'their' appears where the sense requires 'thy' (also Sonnet 35); editors usually assume compositor's misreading of a manuscript abbreviation. A few defend 'their' as referring to the thoughts.

anchor: a jewel hung in ghastly night
title: like a jewel hung in ghastly night
short: The friend's image shines in the dark like a jewel, perhaps the carbuncle, thought to glow by its own light.
body: Renaissance lapidaries held that certain stones, especially the carbuncle, emitted their own light and could shine in darkness, a belief that may lie behind the image. The image of a gem against night recurs in Romeo's 'like a rich jewel in an Ethiop's ear' (Romeo and Juliet 1.5). 'Ghastly' means terrifying, ghost-like; the night is a frightening old woman whose 'old face' (l. 12) becomes 'new' and beautiful in the jewel's light.

title: by day my limbs, by night my mind
short: The couplet balances day against night and body against mind: the lover never rests, for the friend's sake and his own.
body: The couplet's chiastic balance (day/limbs, night/mind; for thee/for myself) neatly summarises the octave. 'For thee' can mean on your account (because of you) and 'for myself' because of my own longing; Booth notes that it also suggests the lover finds no quiet for the friend's benefit, a submissive service. The theme of unrest continues directly in Sonnet 28 ('How can I then return in happy plight / That am debarr'd the benefit of rest?').
